entry.title: MDX Showcase: Custom Components + Design Language
entry.subtitle: Prose and lists, footnotes, carousels, collapsible sections, WIP reveal, ToC, and media presence
entry.excerpt: A working reference post demonstrating our MDX components, styles, and authoring patterns.
entry.content:
This post is a **living reference**: copy/paste any of the snippets below into other posts. On blog and project pages, a **collapsible table of contents** is rendered automatically above the article (from `##`–`####` headings plus `` and `` section titles). You normally should **not** add a second `` inside the MDX. Use `` only when you need a fully manual list inside the body. ## Design language - **Layout**: legacy-inspired blog cards, dashed borders, calm typography. - **Dark mode**: everything should remain readable, with preserved hierarchy. - **MDX blocks**: framed “content widgets” that don’t fight the article text. ## Prose examples: paragraphs and lists ### H3 #### H4 ##### H5 ###### H6 Plain paragraphs are the default: they inherit spacing and color from the article body. Use *emphasis*, **strong**, and `inline code` in the flow of a sentence. A second paragraph shows the usual gap between blocks. For the same underline style as MDX components, use a normal markdown link: [example.com](https://example.com). **Unordered list** (bullets, GFM): - First item with **bold** and a nested level: - Nested bullet one - Nested bullet two - Second top-level item - Third item with a [link inside the list](https://example.com) **Ordered list** (numbered): 1. First step. Numbering is automatic. 2. Second step; lines can wrap when the column is narrow, like this longer sentence that demonstrates wrapping in the article layout. 3. Third step to finish the sequence. **Circled numbers** (no component; plain HTML in MDX). Same padding and spacing as other lists; markers are ①–⑳, then decimal if you go past 20:
  1. Yet, it happened that under the current methodology, “interesting” buildings are often repetitive because of construction patterns (housing blocks, industrial sites, etc.).
  2. Some of the actually most complex structures are not mapped well and need case-by-case handling.
Mixed idea: after a list, another short paragraph resets the rhythm before the next heading. ## Optional collapsible section and paragraphs, blocks, lists, and carousels inside collapsibles Longer sections can live inside **`CollapsibleSection`**: native `
` behavior, with a real heading (`level` **2**, **3**, or **4**) for outline and ToC. The sidebar ToC picks up `title` and `level` from the opening tag, using the same slug as the rendered heading. - `defaultOpen={true}` starts expanded. - Default hints: **Click or tap to open/close section**; override with `hintOpen` / `hintClose` or hide with `showHint={false}`. - Omit duplicate markdown `###` with the same text, or you will get two ToC entries. MDX mixes **markdown** and **JSX**. Block-level JSX (`
…
` split across lines) must sit in its own “paragraph” in the AST: put **blank lines** before the opening tag and after the closing tag. If you glue `
` to prose without a blank line, you can get compile errors like `Expected a closing tag for
… before the end of paragraph`. **Do not put `
` inside a markdown paragraph.** The renderer wraps prose in `

…

`, and `

` cannot contain `

`, which breaks HTML and can cause hydration errors like `Expected server HTML to contain a matching
in

`. For **inline** chips or highlights, use `` (or plain ``) instead; reserve `

` for blocks separated by blank lines. Long posts often put **several paragraphs**, **markdown lists**, **``**, and **``** in the same ``. Use a **blank line** between paragraphs, between a paragraph and a list, and **before and after** block JSX so MDX does not merge invalid nesting. Open the **parent** section below for copy-pasteable **`level={4}`** demos (all under one **`level={3}`** parent). Nested `
` is valid HTML. First paragraph as normal markdown. Second paragraph with a [markdown link](https://example.com) and **strong**. External targets pick up the site link treatment when you use plain markdown: [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/). Tailwind does not scan `content/**/*.mdx`, so prefer **inline styles** or existing global classes for one-off accents. Example: amber callout text beside normal body copy. Combine with italics and `code` as needed. Same-origin paths behave as internal navigation: Blog index. External URLs can use the shared external pattern: Example.com (marker and new tab come from your global styles + attributes). The line above this callout is blank so MDX does not merge the `
` into a paragraph.
Callout or sidebar-style block: put real sentences here. You can wrap multiple lines inside one div; keep blank lines outside the div so MDX does not treat the block as part of a markdown paragraph.
The line below the closing `
` is blank, then this paragraph continues normally. Inline with text: highlight strip - use `` (not `
`) inside markdown paragraphs so the output stays valid `

…

`. For a full-width strip, use a block `
` with blank lines above and below. Short intro in markdown. Block components like `` and `` need the same blank-line discipline: isolate the grid from paragraphs above and below. The **grid** control defaults to **Uniform** (square tiles, like **`/gallery`**). Default **`imageFit` is `none`** for uniform tiles; use **`imageFit="cover"`** to match the gallery, **`imageFit="contain"`** to letterbox (e.g. maps), or set **`grid="variable"`** (or the toolbar) for masonry. After the grid, resume normal markdown. This pattern works in project MDX pages too. Start with a short opener that sets context. Add a second paragraph so you can see vertical rhythm and line length in the collapsible body. Inline links work: [Wikipedia - Markdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markdown). What to verify before you publish: - The list starts after a **blank line** (markdown block boundary), not glued to the previous sentence. - Nested bullets when you need hierarchy: - Child item A - Child item B - A final item with `inline code` and a [link inside the list](https://example.com). Close with a wrap-up paragraph so the section does not end abruptly on a list. That reads better in print and in screen readers. Use a numbered list when order matters, then show figures: 1. Pick stills with different aspect ratios if you want to stress-test layout. 2. Keep captions short; **click an image** to open the lightbox (same behavior as a top-level carousel). After the carousel, explain what the reader should take away from the figures. If you add another list, separate it with a blank line: - Keep blank lines around `` and other block components. - Prefer GFM markdown lists here; use raw `
    ` only when you need custom markup. Square framing works well for thumbnails, UI screenshots, or maps where width and height should feel balanced. Intro paragraph ends here. Closing paragraph: choose `aspect="wide"` (16:9) vs `aspect="square"` (1:1) deliberately so captions line up with your narrative and the figure does not feel cropped or floating. You made it? ## Under construction cover (WipReveal) Blog and project **detail** pages automatically wrap the article body in this cover when frontmatter has `wip: true`, or a `version` that looks like a draft (`draft`, `draft article`, `draft-beta`, …). Title and meta stay clear; click the frosted overlay once to peek. Set `wip: false` to opt out even if `version` mentions draft. You can also wrap **any block** in MDX (blank lines before and after the tags): Pretend this is unfinished work: a short paragraph, a list, and a small image strip sit behind the cover until you click. - Blurred preview of the body - Kicker: **Under construction** - Hint: **Click to peek anyway** Optional props: `kicker`, `title`, `hint`, and `active` (default `true`; use `active={false}` to render children with no cover). ## Optional Interactive footnotes Footnotes can show a preview popover on hover/focus and still work as normal jump links. In longer writing, they are useful for source links, caveats, and small side notes that would otherwise interrupt the paragraph rhythm. Imagine you are describing a migration from legacy HTML to MDX: the main text can stay focused on decisions and outcomes, while footnotes hold implementation details, dates, and external references. This keeps the narrative readable on first pass, but still gives power users context one hover away. You can also use footnotes for "method notes" in data posts: sample size assumptions, API limits, and timing windows. In practice, readers who need those details can open them instantly, and readers who do not can keep moving without losing flow. Basic behavior: hover or focus the superscript reference to preview this text inline. Click still jumps to the footnotes section as a normal anchor. Good editorial use: move low-priority details (naming debates, one-off caveats, timeline precision) into notes so the main paragraph stays clear. External references work too. Example:{' '} interactive footnotes demo. Data-method note example: "Aggregation uses daily snapshots from 2024-01-01 to 2024-03-31; missing dates are forward-filled for visualization continuity." ## Optional Carousel section with modal window Click an image to open it in a modal. Manual attribution while BibTeX still comes from **page frontmatter** (`title`, `date`, `citationAuthor`, optional `citationUrl`): Fully automatic (same frontmatter - no `citation` / `url` props):
